name: Legal
blurb: Research, review, and drafting at scale, the citation-sanction lesson, and the benchmarks and trade bodies that measure legal AI accuracy.

points.desc: The ABA Center for Innovation's AI work, including Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI ethics, is the profession's reference point.
points.name: The ABA carries the profession's guidance

points.desc: The Legal Models section tracks models tuned for legal text, and the lawsuit tracker follows the AI docket itself.

points.name: Vals AI benchmarks legal reasoning

summary: Research, review, and drafting assistance are deployed at scale; sanctions for unverified citations made verification the industry lesson.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's survey of professional, scientific, and technical services, a category that includes legal work, puts the latest share of firms using AI in the last two weeks at 43.3%, up from 41.9% in the prior period. That is the broadest adoption signal in these sources, and none of them offers a legal-only adoption rate.

What legal AI is being bought and built for is clearer. Legaltech Hub reports that OpenAI has released Astra for Law, a configuration of its GPT-6 Astra model paired with legal knowledge, tools, and ecosystem plugins, built initially for Am Law 200 firms. The same directory describes Steno's Transcript Genius for mining deposition and trial transcripts for summaries and strategic insights, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document and pleading verification. ILTA notes Epiq's Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access, and Litify's expansion of ACE with firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity. Stanford CodeX, a partnership between the Law School and the Department of Computer Science, runs programs for agentic AI applications at the intersection of technology and law and builds computational models of legal systems.

Vendor activity concentrates on large-firm workflows and platform integrations, but the sources do not report dollar amounts. Legaltech Hub positions itself as a directory where buyers research, vendors showcase, and investors understand the marketplace, and its coverage of Astra for Law explicitly targets Am Law 200 firms. The World of AI catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads, and release date refreshed daily, which suggests a broad open-model layer beneath the commercial tools.

On ROI and accuracy, the sources are thinner. Vals AI runs private, domain-specific benchmarks in legal, tax, and finance, and its evaluations include legal research among routine knowledge work where some models are slowest, but the excerpts do not give a legal-specific accuracy score or a return-on-investment figure. ILTA says AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs, but it does not quantify purchasing outcomes.

The regulatory and risk posture is more developed. The ABA's Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence focused on six issues: AI and the Profession, AI Risk Management, AI and Access to Justice, AI Governance, AI Challenges ,  Generative AI, and AI and Legal Education. The task force has concluded, and the ABA Center for Innovation continues to address ethical considerations, provide guidance on trustworthy and responsible development and use, and identify strategies to mitigate AI-related risks. Legaltech Hub also flags a training risk: as generative AI takes over document review, first drafts, and due diligence, firms are confronting the loss of the repetitive tasks through which junior lawyers developed judgment, and are experimenting with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those learning opportunities.

A reader deciding whether to deploy should weigh the 43.3% adoption figure in adjacent professional services against the absence of legal-only adoption, ROI, and legal-specific benchmark results in these sources. The tooling is real and expanding, the ABA guidance is available, and the junior-lawyer training concern is a live operational issue, but the evidence base for what works in legal practice remains thinner than the vendor activity suggests.

https://www.iltanet.org/.brief: ILTA describes itself as a global resource community for legal technologists and notes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of large language models, with this spring’s Peer to Peer topics reflecting that evolution. Epiq announced the availability of Model Context Protocol connectors for its Epiq AI, Discover, Narrate, and Access products. Litify expanded its ACE offering with firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity. The page also states that Discovery reads the tools a firm already uses, identifies repeated work, ranks it by hours cost, and turns any finding into automation.

https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/.brief: Legaltech Hub presents itself as a worldwide catalogue of legal technology products and services, aimed at buyers, vendors, and investors. The page notes that OpenAI has released Astra for Law, a configuration of its GPT-6 Astra model tailored for legal work and initially built for Am Law 200 firms. It also highlights Steno’s Transcript Genius, an AI tool for analyzing deposition and trial transcripts, and MiAI Law, an Australian platform combining case law research, legislative research, summarization, contract review, and document verification. A further item examines how generative AI automating document review and first drafts may remove learning opportunities for junior lawyers, and describes firm experiments with simulations and redesigned workflows to rebuild those opportunities.

https://law.stanford.edu/codex-the-stanf.brief: CodeX is a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science that studies how information technology can improve legal processes. It applies data science and artificial intelligence to build quantitative and predictive models of the law, moving beyond traditional empirical analysis. The program offers a hands-on accelerated track for interdisciplinary student teams to prototype Agentic AI and the CFAA applications at the intersection of technology and law. CodeX also hosts a hackathon that brings together AI innovators, machine learning specialists, and legal professionals to prototype future legal technology. Additionally, it organizes an international conference and FutureLaw 2026 to bring together leaders in law, technology, and policy to discuss sustainable, ethical, and responsible AI in legal systems.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page reports that it lists the 1,000 most-downloaded open legal models on Hugging Face Hub, showing licence, download counts, and release dates, refreshed daily. It also lists books by Stephen R. Jordan, including “The Operating Discipline for AI Library™” series, now available on Amazon. Additionally, the page catalogs several AI audit and assessment tools such as the AI Business Enablement Audit™, AI Readiness & Performance Assessment™, AI Risk & Governance Review™, AI Efficiency & Process Optimization™, AI IT Security Audit™, AI IT Security Implementation & Strategy™, Secure by Design in the Age of AI™, Application Security in the Age of AI™, and The AI Lawyer.

https://www.americanbar.org/groups/cente.brief: The Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has finished its work, and the Center for Innovation will keep addressing how AI affects the legal profession, including ethical issues, trustworthy development, and risk-mitigation strategies. It will also provide guidance on responsible AI use. Past webinars from the Task Force examine how AI is reshaping law practice, covering practical applications, new legal technology, and the ethical, professional-responsibility, and regulatory challenges lawyers must navigate.
